questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-7)-9\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $S$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3.$ Find the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/957c59d27a871a52f110c3dca91cec390091c13ceba6e14d6485f92aa150c51a.svg)

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/6095f1a65a9b9b245de2dd4cad611d2616a2b3b15e4701fe33c3c53b913c2283.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consists of the vectors $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2,$ and $\mathbf e_3,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/41bd0d4956d8ec09d0339a79329c6739e07e698d9dee9f192968d77c9ec28842.svg)

The components of the vectors in $\mathcal{B}$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/30a1bdc2316f5d7acc527cb1d69fc11c7b732f9e22a4d57a11ed84f2db1e3cd5.svg)

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{S}.$ 

Therefore, we obtain
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/5606e00ccc39829e3c599aa86286dcc1f1cb4e3febb280adf4e1bbe18dc7ab6a.svg)

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=0,$ and $c=10.$

                    Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/4676de86bd5b4bc2a8e1d6a9432379d0769163113913137f8143a71eb16e8240.svg)
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} & -3 \\ \frac{3}{2} & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V,$ the **change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$.

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/062187705e6074afa6b5356be64f8deb878be540e2c3b236b22dbd244b872cc6.svg)

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.
$$

If we happen to know that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/32409a45b5ebcf6b8c1cc43404126b514066ace8d8c71bcec2e99f759833ec84.svg) 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

This can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ede6eb17f0667a8974902bf2d181150eeb3c665faa3059bb818bb9a61b631511.png)

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Given two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V,$ the **change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$.

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/062187705e6074afa6b5356be64f8deb878be540e2c3b236b22dbd244b872cc6.svg)

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.
$$

If we happen to know that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/32409a45b5ebcf6b8c1cc43404126b514066ace8d8c71bcec2e99f759833ec84.svg) 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

This can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ede6eb17f0667a8974902bf2d181150eeb3c665faa3059bb818bb9a61b631511.png)

tutorials.name: The Inverse of a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
tutorials.problem:
Since the columns of a change-of-coordinates matrix are linearly independent, the matrix must be invertible.

In fact, the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}
	\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
	P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$

tutorials.title: The Inverse of a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
tutorials.content:
Since the columns of a change-of-coordinates matrix are linearly independent, the matrix must be invertible.

In fact, the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}
	\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
	P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$
